toc.title: Putting it into your daily life

sections.title: Set things up for the state you lean into
Notice your state, then ask what you can do from it

blocks.p: You're trying to get more done. Maybe you're an artist, or starting a new hobby, or you just want to be more productive at work. But it's hard to focus, you lack energy, or sometimes you just don't feel like it. The answer might be making use of what your nervous system has to offer in the present moment.

Your nervous system is your body's communication and control center. It regulates the automatic things you don't have to think about, like breathing and heartbeat, while also supporting your thinking, your decision making, and your emotional regulation. It can be in different states, and those states change throughout the day, moment to moment. Understanding them can help you manage your energy and focus, and even be more productive. Let's go through the three states and how to get the most from each one.

blocks.h: The three states, and the mixes

blocks.p: Here's the brief version of the Polyvagal Theory. Mammals can be in one of three states: safety, flight or fight, or shutdown. In other words, connection, mobility, or immobility. It's more complex than that, and we'll touch on that, but that's the base.

ul: Safety is about connection to self, others, and environment.
Shutdown is about immobilizing: playing dead in the face of a life threat.

blocks.p: These states can also combine into mixed states, just like primary colors: red and blue make purple.

ul: Play is safety plus flight or fight: connection plus mobility.
Stillness is safety plus shutdown: connection plus immobility. That's the ability to be alone and immobile and be okay with it.
Freeze is flight or fight plus shutdown: you're charged up but immobile at the same time. It's like having the gas and the brake on at the same time. The wheels just spin.

blocks.p: All of these come from biological pathways. They're not just feelings floating around inside of us. Our emotions and thoughts come from the state of our body, and we can feel these states when they're active, if we're mindful enough. It's not a guessing game. So the question is how to notice when each one is active, and how to get the most benefit from it while it is.

The safety state comes from the ventral vagal pathways in your brainstem. It's known as the social engagement system. When it's active, we can make eye contact, smile, hug, be close to each other, use gentle touch. Without it, you can't really do those things, or if you do, they won't feel good. They won't feel safe. It's active when we have safe enough people and safe enough places.

Safety is ideal for creativity, connection, and optimal performance. With enough of it, you can do a wider variety of things. You can think critically and weigh pros and cons. You can map out an agenda for a project. You can work well with others: hear what they think and feel with empathy, share what you think and feel, and come to a compromise that meets your goals. You can plan which colors to mix to get a certain color in a painting, or work out the best way to edit the words in a book to get a point across. From safety, you have access to thought, but also to the present moment, to yourself, to others, and to emotion.

So when it comes to productivity, creativity, and getting stuff done, we want as much access to safety as possible. That doesn't mean sitting cross-legged with your eyes closed, meditating. As long as you have enough safety, you can simply focus and get stuff done.
There's no prescription for this. I don't know exactly what will bring up your safety state. But there are some pretty predictable things you can do:

ol: Extend your exhale. Whatever state you're in, be mindful of your inhale, and then make the exhale a little longer. That brings in the parasympathetic nervous system, which is where the safety state lives, and helps you settle into the present moment. While you extend that exhale, add a little something: say something kind to yourself, or remind yourself what you're working on.

Be mindful of your movement and your senses. Whatever you're doing right now, be mindful of it. If you go for a walk, notice the movement of walking. If you're painting or sketching, notice the movement of your arm, your elbow, your shoulder, whether it's fast or slow. And notice the sensory input: the vibrancy of the color, what it feels like to flex and release, what you smell, hear, and see.

Bring in elements of nature. I don't expect you to stop what you're doing and go hike in a forest. But open your blinds and let natural light in. If you can, sit by a window and look outside while you work. I love to do that. Use sound: I like rain in the background, especially when I'm slower paced and settling into stillness. It grounds me. Use smell: a candle that smells like the forest isn't the forest, but it's a step closer.

Connect with safe others. You don't have to be best friends with everyone you work with. But can you exchange a smile? Some chit chat about the weekend? I personally hate it, but there's benefit to it. When someone is in a safe enough state, their voice naturally takes on a sing-song quality that goes down and up and everywhere in between. That's vocal prosody, and when we hear it, it nudges us into our safety state a bit more.

blocks.p: If you work alone, first off, get out of the house as much as you can. Smile at somebody at the coffee shop or on your walk around the block, say hello, hear their voice. If you can't, listen to voices in music. Rap and heavy metal are less than ideal here, with screaming and a lot of monotone. Something like the Beach Boys or Etta James has a lot more vocal prosody. On a break, when you listen to a podcast or a video, can you connect with the person's voice? Can you hear the safety in it? Can you see their face and mindfully notice how that feels inside you?
You don't need the perfect natural environment or the perfect co-regulating person. You can bring elements of these into your workday or your creative process to feel a little safer than before.

You'll feel it. It can feel like calm and relaxation. It can also feel like excitement and productivity, curiosity, interest. All of these involve being connected to the present moment. If you can pause, look out the window, and just take in the present moment, you're in your safety state.
Thought is another way to recognize it. Thinking critically, weighing pros and cons, planning step by step: all of these involve some safety.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.p: Now let's shift to sympathetic activation, which you probably know as flight or fight. It's not that simple. I want you to associate the sympathetic nervous system with mobility, not just flight or fight.

Flight or fight becomes relevant when we don't have access to literal safety. In actual danger, your body will use it, and in that moment it isn't accessing its own safety state, because the environment demands that it run away or be aggressive. But when there's enough safety in the system, we can also use sympathetic mobility. Safety plus sympathetic gives you playfulness, creativity, productivity, and motivation. That's a lot different from flight or fight, which is about getting away or being aggressive.

Sympathetic mobility is great for short bursts. If you're painting, you'll use stronger, more forceful brushstrokes, maybe splashing things on the canvas. If you're sketching, your hand, wrist, elbow, and shoulder move faster. At work, you get a ton done all at once, typing really fast. That's great.

But we also want longer, drawn-out periods of motivation, and that comes from your safety state being more active along with your sympathetic state, the two balancing each other out. That gives you productivity that's more sustainable. With less safety, you get bursts, and then perhaps a collapse into shutdown: burst, shut down, burst, shut down. A lot of good can come from that, but we want more safety, to draw out the motivation, productivity, and creativity.

Without safety, it's more scattered. Ideas and inspiration pop up here and there, but they're not predictable, and it feels more out of control and sporadic. When the inspiration is there, you try to capture it and make the most of it, and there's nothing wrong with that. With more safety, it won't be as sporadic. You'll have more intentionality over it.
So how do you use your sympathetic mobility on purpose?

Option one: procrastination. You're probably doing this already, and I've been there too. The longer you wait, the more it builds, and eventually you just have to get the thing done. No shame. I've gotten through a lot of my life this way, and it has its usefulness. You wait until the sympathetic energy builds so much that you complete whatever you're working on.

Option two: structure. This is the one I recommend more. Set goals and funnel your energy in a specific direction. Instead of waiting for the deadline and using that procrastination energy, can you do a little each day toward the goal? You probably can. Will you? That's another discussion. With more safety in your system, I think you're more likely to. If you lean into defensive activation, more flight or fight or even shutdown, you're probably less likely. So this really comes down to how much you're practicing being in your safety state, and how much of it you bring into your creative and productive process.

Within that second option, set small to medium achievements toward the big goal. Say the big goal is a slideshow presentation. Day to day, the achievements are: What design do I like? What font and colors am I pulled toward? Do I have enough sources? How many slides, what layout? How long will it be? Instead of sitting down to figure out how to achieve the big goal, you're working on one achievement at a time. Make a list and start knocking them off, and all of a sudden you're making progress on the bigger goal.

If you sit down to work with nothing but sympathetic activation, it goes here and there and everywhere. You'll be distracted and pulled in every direction. An achievement list creates a funnel toward your goal.

The image in my mind is Luke in the X-wing, about to blow up the Death Star. Before the trench, he's just flying out in space. He could go anywhere. But once he knows the goal, the ventilation shaft connected to the trench, he flies down into the trench, through it, and fires his missile into the shaft. That trench funnels his energy, his activation, toward one specific goal. You can do that every day toward a larger goal, like a painting or a presentation.

blocks.h3: Music to stay in the trench

blocks.p: Say you have your big goal and your achievement list, and you're working at it, but you notice you're being pulled this way and that. When you're in a sympathetic state, music can really help focus your energy in the present moment in a specific direction. You could use music to get up and dance out some energy, then sit down and focus better. Or use it as a beat, the rhythm to get stuff done.

I love listening to chill hop when I'm trying to focus but I'm also kind of amped up. It has a beat and no vocals, often little sounds of nature mixed in, and that lo-fi crackly sound I find really soothing. With energy and chill hop, I'm way more focused and get way more done. Same with working out: you know what music helps you stay down that trench. For me, rap does not help me work out whatsoever. Heavy metal does.

Mobility without enough safety can feel like anxiety or anger. So look out, mindfully, for an increased heart rate, some muscle tension, rapid breathing, thoughts going all over the place. Those are good signs you have more sympathetic activation, more mobility, than safety.

We just want to balance those out. First, put music on, set an agenda, and see how it goes. If it's still too much, get up and move. Let some of that energy out and bring it down a notch. Do it mindfully if you can: if you go for a walk, listen, look, smell, use your senses, smile at people, pet a dog (ask first if it belongs to someone). Let your mobilization come down enough and your safety come up enough to balance out. Then sit down with your achievement list, your bigger goal in mind, and start knocking things off.
Now the third primary state, shutdown. Shutdown happens when we can't be safe, we can't run away, and we can't fight. So the body collapses. It plays dead, basically, in the face of a life threat.

This is a necessary part of being alive. All organisms have some form of immobility that has helped them survive over generations and generations, passing their genetic material to the next generation, which then uses it to survive, and so on. So normalize it. It's a part of you, a part of me, a part of all of us. And we can actually use it to our advantage in daily life.

I want you to view shutdown not as defeat and not as a defect. We need to collapse in our daily life. We need to collapse and restore, to get ready for the next day or the next project. It's an opportunity to rest and reconnect with ourselves, our environment, and maybe others. You've had a day of productivity, good or bad, and at the end of it you need to collapse, maybe shut down. That prepares you for the next day. Think of it as a necessary part of your productivity and creativity cycle. We have to have downtime, rest, and reconnection.

blocks.h3: When there's a lot of shutdown

blocks.p: You might spend a lot of time in shutdown, and it looks like depression. I'd say it is depression. You might spend a lot of time isolating. Okay, that's fair. What that tells me is that you need to listen to your body's needs and bring more elements of safety into your daily life, and that might just be reconnecting to the outside environment using your senses. With a lot of shutdown, you probably need lower stimulation, more alone time, and to reconnect to your environment through your senses.

As you allow for that and give yourself true moments of recovery, it's more restoring than anything else. Not phone binging, not food binging, not drugs, not fake it till you make it. True rest and recovery, true solitude and quiet. It's okay to listen to your body's needs, provide for them, and then slowly come out of shutdown. Eventually you'll work your way into mobility, into some sympathetic activation.

You'll know there's too much shutdown because you'll feel numb, dissociated, collapsed, withdrawn. That tells me there's too much shutdown and not enough safety. Again, listen to your body's needs. Plowing through work and forcing yourself into exercise and productivity is fine, but it only lasts so long. Eventually you burn out or collapse, because you're not listening to what your body needs.

So instead of chasing tons of mobility and productivity, strive for stillness. Stillness is shutdown plus safety. Mindfully bring more elements of safety into your life, and then mindfully allow yourself to be in shutdown. When those two combine, you get stillness. And from stillness, mobilization may emerge.

I think that's a really good flow: shutdown, to stillness, to sympathetic. If you're not bringing safety into your shutdown to get to stillness, you might be setting yourself up for failure over and over. The safety piece is kind of necessary. Without it, you might cycle between shutdown and flight or fight. It can feel like deep depression and then sudden surges of fight activation, maybe anxiety, but more likely irritability, anger, maybe rage. Depression to anger and back again. That's when there's too much shutdown.
Deb Dana named why stillness takes safety when she was on the podcast:

q: Stillness is the most complicated autonomic blend of states, because how do you come into quiet, into stillness, without stimulating shut down? It's a tricky thing to do, especially for people with a trauma history. Because stillness is a very vulnerable place and I have to really feel safe to come into stillness.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana Interview: Story Follows State, Climbing the Ladder and Diagnosing (episode 29)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c)

blocks.p: The other immobility option is freeze: shutdown plus flight or fight. Freeze is different. It can include numbness and dissociation, but there's also mobility in there, activation. Freeze can feel like stress and a lot of overwhelm. It can feel like panic. It can feel like rage.
So connect with safety first, which thaws the freeze and its frozen flight or fight activation, and then use that activation toward creativity, productivity, exercise, whatever you want to do.

You can reduce your fear through small, manageable steps. With a lot of freeze, saying "I'm going to create this wonderful slideshow all at once" isn't realistic, and it will probably reinforce your freeze. It's too much all at once. It demands too much safety and too much mobility. So make the goals really small. It's great to want to finish that painting, or go to the gym every day for thirty minutes. But can you do that now and tomorrow, and sustain it long term? Maybe not.

So instead of thirty minutes, can you lift a weight at home for two minutes? Can you spend thirty seconds visualizing working out? Do those teeny tiny goals for a week, then add to the challenge. "I can visualize going to the gym for thirty seconds a day for a week. Can I now drive to the gym, get out of my car, get back in, and drive home? Can I do that for a week?" And the week after that, can you go into the gym and just stand there for a couple of minutes? That sounds weird, I know, but you get the idea. Small steps toward the bigger goal are more likely to happen, even from freeze, than an unreachable, huge goal.
And for shutdown: if you've earned that collapse at the end of the day, go ahead and collapse. Fall face first onto your bed, in quiet, and just breathe and recover from the day.

blocks.h: Putting it into your daily life

blocks.p: Now, how do you take what you know and put it into your life in a way that works for you? I want you to streamline your efforts as much as possible, and make it easy to move through these states and use each one well.

blocks.h3: Set things up for the state you lean into

blocks.p: If you know that more often than not you need to collapse and decompress, do you have a place for that, ready for you? If not, preparing one might be a good place to start.

If you want to be more productive, and that means reading and studying for a test, is your book ready to go? Or is it in a backpack in your closet? Would it be easier to keep it in the spot where you'll do the most reading, the most stillness-inducing spot in your home, waiting for you, instead of going through the obstacles of backpack, closet, and across the house?

If you have more mobility in your system, do you have your structure, your achievement list to mark off? Is it easy to get to? I turned a closet in my office into a chalkboard and storage area. The chalkboard has my priorities, listed and grouped, to help me structure my time and get my priorities done before I move on to the next things, which is way too much. But it helps me focus. All I have to do is look up to my left and I see my list. Is yours easy to get to, or is there an obstacle in the way? Even picking up your phone and opening an app to look at your notes is an obstacle. Is there an easier way? Can you put sticky notes on your screen?
The basic idea: if you know you lean into a certain state, are things set up so you can easily make use of what that state has to offer?

I highly recommend practicing feeling safe every single day, and I don't think it has to be much. In my community, I've been giving out really small challenges that take no more than two minutes of mindfulness.
One week, the challenge was to pick the same spot at the same time every day, set a timer for up to two minutes, and just listen and feel, look inward, and connect with the outside world.

The next week, you set an alarm for a different time each day for five days. When it goes off, you spend up to two minutes being mindful. One of my alarms went off when I was in CVS, so I used two minutes to walk up and down the aisles, touch things, smell candles, and connect with the environment. Another went off when I was at a friend's house in the middle of a Dungeons and Dragons game, and it was incredibly hard to be mindful because we were having so much fun. So it didn't work out right then. But later that night, chatting with my friend under the stars, I used the moment to be mindful of the absolute serenity of it.

No, it doesn't solve all your problems. I know that. But it starts to create predictability. It creates a reference point for safety. If you can do thirty seconds, you can do two minutes. And if you can do two minutes, what else can you accomplish after that?

blocks.h3: Notice your state, then ask what you can do from it

blocks.p: The last recommendation: look inward and notice what state you're in. Do you have more mobility or less? More collapse or less? More potential to connect or less? For now, just notice what you have more or less of throughout the day.

If you can do that, you can ask yourself: what can I accomplish from this activation, or lack of it? What's the best I can do in this moment? Is this a time to collapse and be okay with it for five minutes? A time to look at my achievement list and start knocking things off one by one? Or a chance to take a break, go hug my kids and say I love you, and then get back to work?
